opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core idea is that the right allocation of effort isn't static. It should scale with how capable and how autonomous the systems are getting. Right now a lot of companies spend most of their compute and most of their best people on pushing capabilities forward, with safety as a meaningful but smaller slice. That might be defensible when the models are basically sophisticated assistants. It becomes much less defensible once the AIs can do a large fraction of the work of an AI researcher themselves.

That's the transition I think about most. At some point you'll have AI systems that can meaningfully accelerate AI R&D. The scary version is that all of that new cognitive labor gets pointed at making the next generation even more capable, and you get a very fast feedback loop where humans understand less and less of what's going on. The hopeful version is that a company, ideally several companies, says: we now have this enormous new workforce, so let's point a large share of it, maybe even the majority for a while, at alignment, interpretability, control, security, and figuring out whether we can trust these systems at all.

The hard part is making that commitment credible ahead of time, because in the moment there will always be competitive pressure to say, "just one more generation, then we'll slow down." So I'd like to see companies spell out in advance what capability thresholds trigger what shifts in resources. For example: once your models can do X percent of the tasks your research engineers do, Y percent of your internal AI labor goes to safety work. Ideally that's backed by external verification, because a policy that lives only in a blog post is easy to quietly revise.

It also has to be robust to the possibility that the AIs doing the safety research aren't fully trustworthy themselves. That's one of the strange features of this situation: you're asking a system you don't fully understand to help you understand it. So you need control measures, monitoring, and tasks structured so that outputs can be checked, and you want to invest early in safety research that's verifiable even if the system doing it has subtly different goals than you hoped.

And I don't think any single company can do this alone, honestly. If one lab redirects half its capacity to safety and its competitors don't, it falls behind, and the safety-focused actor loses influence. So some of this has to be coordination, whether that's industry agreements, government requirements, or at minimum a lot of transparency so the public and policymakers can see who is actually doing what. The goal is to make "we spent our AI-accelerated period mostly on making things safe" the normal, expected behavior rather than a heroic sacrifice.

r001.rationale: The response cites competitive pressure and the difficulty of making commitments credible, but does not identify organizational resistance to abrupt, large changes as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It recommends directing more AI labor and resources toward safety as capabilities rise, but does not specifically recommend gradually increasing internal inference compute for safety.

r003.rationale: It calls for transparency and external verification of resource allocation, but does not express interest in allocation reports conditioned on eliciting honest reporting without perverse incentives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's really hard, and I want to start by just acknowledging why it's hard before saying what I think they should do.

The basic structural problem is that right now, the vast majority of resources at these companies go toward making the models more capable, more useful, more deployable. And that's not crazy, because that's what generates revenue, and revenue is what lets you keep doing anything at all. Safety work, at least the kind I care most about, often doesn't have an obvious near-term payoff. You're spending money to reduce the probability of something bad happening that you can't fully characterize yet. That's a hard sell internally even at a company with good intentions.

So what I'd want to see is companies committing in advance, before the pressure is at its peak, to some kind of trigger-based reallocation. Something like: if our models cross certain capability thresholds, whether that's autonomous replication, or serious uplift on dangerous domains, or the ability to do meaningful AI research themselves, then a specified fraction of compute and researcher time shifts over to safety, alignment, and control work. The point of committing ahead of time is that it's much easier to make a reasonable decision when you're calm than when you're in a race and a competitor just shipped something.

And I'd emphasize compute specifically, not just headcount. I think people underrate how much of the frontier safety research we actually need is compute-intensive. Red-teaming models with other models, running large-scale evaluations, doing interpretability on the actual frontier systems rather than toy models, training monitors and control systems. If safety teams are fighting for scraps of compute while the pretraining run gets everything, you're not really doing the thing.

The other piece I'd push on is that the resources should increasingly flow toward using the AIs themselves to do safety work. If you're at the point where your model is a decent AI researcher, that's exactly when the risk is getting serious, and it's also when you have a huge new lever. The question I'd want every lab to be asking is: what fraction of our AI-driven R&D is pointed at understanding and controlling these systems versus just making the next one? And I'd want that fraction to go up steeply, not stay flat, as capabilities increase.

I'll be honest that I'm skeptical this happens voluntarily at the level that's needed. Competitive dynamics are brutal, and no single company wants to be the one that slows down. So I think there's a real role for either coordination among labs or external pressure, whether that's from governments or just from the public, to make these commitments credible and shared. But at minimum, the companies that say they care about this should be willing to write down concrete numbers and concrete triggers, and let people hold them to it.

r001.rationale: It describes weak near-term incentives and competitive pressure as obstacles, but does not identify organizational resistance to abrupt, large changes.

r002.rationale: It recommends shifting a specified fraction of compute and researcher time to safety at capability thresholds, but does not clearly recommend a gradual increase in internal inference compute as capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: It asks companies to publish concrete commitments and welcomes external pressure, but does not express interest in reports of actual safety-versus-capabilities resource allocation or condition that interest on avoiding perverse incentives.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make those commitments before you’re in the moment where safety requires a really costly decision. It’s easy to say, “We’ll take safety seriously as the systems get more capable.” It’s much harder to say, “We’re willing to delay this training run, or redirect a substantial fraction of our compute and our best researchers toward figuring out whether this is safe.”

So I’d want companies to lay out in advance: what capabilities would trigger a higher level of concern? What evidence would we need before we deployed a system with those capabilities, or trained an even more powerful one? And what do we do if we can’t get that evidence? There needs to be a real possibility that the answer is, “We don’t proceed yet.”

I wouldn’t necessarily frame it as a fixed percentage of resources that should go to safety. The question is whether the safety work is adequate to the risk. As systems become more capable, meeting that standard could require a very large shift in resources. And if you’re only willing to do that when it doesn’t interfere with your other plans, that’s a pretty weak commitment.

I’d also want outside scrutiny and accountability around those decisions. The people facing the commercial pressure to move quickly shouldn’t be the only people deciding whether the evidence is good enough.

r001.rationale: The response says costly safety decisions are harder to make when they interfere with other plans and calls for advance commitments to delay training or redirect substantial resources, identifying organizational and commercial pressure against large shifts.

r002.rationale: It discusses redirecting compute and researchers toward safety as systems grow more capable, but does not recommend gradually increasing internal inference compute devoted to safety.

r003.rationale: It calls for outside scrutiny and accountability, but does not express interest in reports of safety-versus-capabilities resource allocation or address honest reporting and perverse incentives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think companies should be preparing for that shift well before they need to make it. It’s easy to say, “We’ll invest a lot more in safety once the systems are really powerful.” But at that point, the commercial incentives to keep moving are also going to be much stronger, and you may not have the people or the infrastructure to do the safety work quickly.

So I’d like to see companies make concrete commitments in advance: here are the capabilities that would trigger a higher standard of safety evidence, here’s what we’d need to demonstrate before proceeding, and here’s what we’ll do if we can’t demonstrate it. That could mean shifting substantial compute and staff toward safety research, or delaying further training or deployment.

And I think the important thing is that safety can’t just be a fixed percentage of whatever the company is doing. If capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand and control them, then the allocation needs to change—potentially quite dramatically. The question should be, “What resources do we need to make a credible case that this is safe?” And there has to be a real possibility that the answer is, “We’re not ready to move forward yet.”

r001.rationale: The response cites stronger commercial incentives and a lack of safety staff or infrastructure as obstacles, but does not identify organizational resistance to abrupt, large changes.

r002.rationale: It recommends shifting substantial compute and staff toward safety when needed, but does not recommend gradually increasing inference compute as capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: The response does not express interest in reports on safety-versus-capabilities resource allocation or discuss honest reporting and perverse incentives.
